case_study_insert.main_stem: Meridian Valley Health (MVH) is a private limited company in the healthcare sector, operating a group of private day-surgery clinics with a workforce of 120. Founded in 2009 by Dr Priya Nair, the business uses a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership. MVH plans to invest $900,000 in a new day-surgery operating theatre and diagnostic imaging suite, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $288,000 a year, a variable cost of $54 a unit and a selling price of $90, and currently produces 14,000 units a year. MVH faces two problems: nurse absenteeism has reached 8% and patient waiting times for diagnostics are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report - Q3 2025: The day-surgery unit performed 3,200 procedures last quarter at a surgical rework rate of 2.4%, down from 4.0% a year ago. Patient complaints fell from 46 to 19 per month. Average waiting time for a diagnostics appointment is 18 days. A survey of 750 patients found that 68% would pay $15 more for same-day diagnostics and 57% choose a provider on its waiting-time reputation. A skills audit shows 30 of 120 clinical staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new imaging machines; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $1,100 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Meridian Valley Health for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.68 to $14.50 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Medical supply and pharmaceutical input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while consumer spending on private healthcare grew 4.2% over the same period.

questions.question_text: MVH plans to fund part of its $900,000 day-surgery expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MVH of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs MVH no interest or capital repayments, protecting cash flow and margins while it already services a $600,000 bank loan and carries fixed costs of $288,000 a year. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 9.6% rise in medical supply costs without pushing the $90 procedure price above what patients will pay.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids collateral and default risk, so the $300,000 is available without putting the new operating theatre at risk of repossession if demand for day surgery disappoints. It also preserves Dr Priya Nair's ownership and control, since no lender can impose covenants on how the diagnostic imaging suite is run or expanded next year.

Because the $300,000 is internal, MVH keeps its debt burden modest while revenue grows from $2,400,000 to $2,900,000, which strengthens its standing with the lender and leaves room for future borrowing if the imaging suite needs a second phase. It also means the 8% nurse absenteeism and any dip in the 14,000-procedure volume do not coincide with a fixed repayment schedule, protecting the group's ability to fund the $1,100 retraining and the same-day diagnostics launch from existing cash.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to MVH's expansion, loan and cost data.

questions.question_text: MVH is launching its new same-day diagnostics service. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship or social media influencer marketing. Which should MVH choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television: A national TV campaign builds rapid, mass awareness of same-day diagnostics across all MVH clinic sites. However, airtime and production are extremely expensive for a 120-staff healthcare group funding a $900,000 expansion, and much of the audience lives outside MVH's regional catchment or never needs private day surgery, so spending would be heavily wasted.

Local radio: Local radio is far cheaper and suits time-sensitive messages such as shorter waiting times, reaching MVH's regional patients directly. Its weakness is narrow reach: the new imaging suite must attract enough scans to cover $288,000 of fixed costs, and local listeners alone cannot deliver the 14,000-unit volume the group targets.

Social media influencer marketing: Health and family lifestyle influencers reach exactly the 68% of 750 surveyed patients who would pay $15 more for same-day diagnostics and the 57% who choose on waiting-time reputation. Engagement is measurable and cost per reached patient is low, though results build more slowly than TV and depend on influencer credibility.

Cost is decisive for a 120-staff group whose 2025 operating profit is $522,000: a national television campaign could absorb a large share of that profit, whereas influencer fees can be capped and measured against the 3,200 procedures handled each quarter. MVH should also track how many of the 57% who value waiting-time reputation actually book, so the campaign is judged against the $36 contribution per scan rather than reach alone.

Recommendation: MVH should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the exact segment in the survey, scales nationally unlike local radio, and costs a fraction of television. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; radio is rejected as too narrow for the imaging suite's volume needs, so MVH should add modest clinic-based referral promotion to convert the influencer interest.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to MVH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MVH with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in MVH's context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and local radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: MVH's nurse absenteeism has reached 8% and patient waiting times are rising. Explain two benefits for MVH of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its clinical teams.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives MVH's 120 staff a genuine voice in how the new day-surgery theatre is organised, raising job satisfaction and addressing the social and esteem needs in Maslow's hierarchy. Nurses who help set imaging-room rotas are likelier to attend reliably, directly reducing the 8% absenteeism that is lengthening waiting times.

Point 2: Consulting the clinicians who handle scans daily generates practical ideas that cut the 2.4% rework rate further and protect the 14,000-unit procedure target. Higher involvement raises commitment and lowers labour turnover, avoiding repeated $1,100 per employee retraining and keeping the diagnostic suite productive while the new service beds in.

Democratic leadership also fits MVH's hierarchical clinical structure because consultants and nurses hold different expertise; consulting both levels produces safer rotas for the 3,200 procedures delivered last quarter. Higher morale reduces the need for agency cover, whose cost would otherwise consume the $36 contribution on each scan, and a stable team protects the 45.0% gross margin reported for 2025. Sustained attendance is therefore both a quality and a financial safeguard for the $900,000 operating theatre.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to MVH's absenteeism, quality and output.

questions.question_text: MVH must upskill 30 clinical staff to operate the new imaging machines. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should MVH choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the imaging suite is specific to MVH's own machines and quality standards, costs no course fees and keeps the 30 staff productive while they learn, protecting the Q3 output of 3,200 procedures and the fall in rework to 2.4%. Drawbacks are that trainer-nurses sacrifice their own work, bad habits can spread, and formal certification is limited if clinical auditors require records.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $1,100 per employee gives structured skills and a recognised certificate for 30 staff, costing $33,000 in total - small beside the $900,000 investment. It withdraws 30 of 120 staff from the line, cutting short-term capacity, and generic content may not match MVH's exact scanner settings, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Quality assurance is a further consideration: a recognised college certificate may be valued by clinical auditors, but the insert gives no evidence that MVH's regulators require one, so the cheaper machine-specific route is not thereby disqualified. An on-the-job programme can be delivered in short sessions around the 18-day diagnostic waiting list, whereas a college timetable removes staff at fixed times and would slow the 3,200-procedure quarter. Blended delivery keeps the $33,000 cost optional.

Decision: MVH should choose on-the-job training first, backed by short college sessions for lead operators. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing capacity while nurse absenteeism is 8%; full off-the-job training is rejected because a $33,000 fee and 30 staff off the ward would disrupt the diagnostic waiting-time target, and college modules can be added later once the suite stabilises.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MVH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in MVH's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in MVH's context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MVH's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $288,000 ÷ ($90 − $54) = $288,000 ÷ $36 = 8,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 8,000 procedures a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $90 − $54 = $36. Answer: contribution per unit is $36.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MVH's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 8,000-unit break-even point with actual output of 14,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 6,000 procedures, to judge whether the new operating theatre is utilisation-ready.
2. Use contribution of $36 to model a discount for insurers: a $6 reduction to $84 leaves $30 contribution, still covering the $288,000 fixed costs at 14,000 units.
3. Set volume targets that service the $600,000 bank loan and justify the $900,000 investment to Dr Priya Nair before committing further capital.
4. Track average total cost of $74.57 ($288,000 ÷ 14,000 + $54) each quarter to spot waste or rework and to test whether the 9.6% input-cost rise is being absorbed.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 8,000 procedures | (ii) Contribution per unit = $36 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety vs 14,000-unit output; pricing/discount modelling vs $288,000 fixed costs; loan servicing for the $900,000 expansion; and average total cost of $74.57 to monitor waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid, contextual use in (iii) (max 4).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MVH's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has MVH's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: In 2024 gross profit of $960,000 on revenue of $2,400,000 is 40.0%; in 2025 gross profit of $1,305,000 on revenue of $2,900,000 is 45.0%. Operating profit of $360,000 in 2024 equals 15.0% of revenue and 18.0% of the $2,000,000 capital employed; in 2025 operating profit of $522,000 is 18.0% of revenue and 22.5% of the $2,320,000 capital employed. Cost of sales rose from $1,440,000 to $1,595,000 while revenue grew faster.

Evaluation: All three measures moved favourably. Gross margins widened from 40.0% to 45.0%, showing better control of clinical supply costs; operating margins rose from 15.0% to 18.0%, so more of each revenue dollar reaches operating profit; and returns on capital employed increased from 18.0% to 22.5%, meaning the existing asset base is working harder. The 6th row, interest payable, rose from $40,000 to $55,000, so the $600,000 loan is a small but growing burden, and a 9.6% input-cost rise could reverse the gross-margin gain in 2026.

The $55,000 interest payable in 2025 is still small relative to $522,000 operating profit, so financing costs do not overturn the improvement, though the rising 9.6% input costs deserve close monitoring.

Conclusion: MVH's financial position has improved on every permitted measure, and the improvement is not merely a revenue effect because margins and capital returns both rose. The residual risk is rising interest and input costs, so management should protect the 45.0% gross margin before the $900,000 expansion loads more capital into the business.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of margin, cost and capital movements and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MVH of offering the $15 same-day diagnostics premium identified in its patient survey.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 750 patients shows 68% would pay $15 more for same-day diagnostics and 57% choose on waiting-time reputation, so a premium raises revenue per scan and protects the $36 contribution per procedure even as medical input costs rise 9.6%. It also reinforces MVH's reputation for shortening the current 18-day wait, strengthening its private-hospital brand.

Disadvantage: Some patients will reject the $15 premium and switch to rivals, reducing the 14,000-unit volume needed to justify the $900,000 imaging suite. Delivering same-day scans may also raise the 2.4% rework rate if clinical staff are rushed, increasing costs and pressure on nurse absenteeism already at 8%.

MVH can also use the premium to fund faster scanner maintenance, which reduces the 18-day waiting time that drives the 57% reputation effect and protects the 2.4% rework rate. However, a two-tier service could create equity concerns in healthcare and distract from the core day-surgery volume needed to cover $288,000 of fixed costs; management should therefore pilot the $15 premium on a single imaging suite and compare contribution before rolling it out across all clinics.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to MVH's survey data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in medical supply input costs will affect MVH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If MVH's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.0075 × $600,000 = $4,500 a year, modest beside $288,000 of fixed costs; if the loan is fixed, the direct cost is zero. Higher rates may also deter patients financing treatment and raise future borrowing costs, and MVH can limit this by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $14.50 an hour): With a workforce of 120 and many hourly-paid support and nursing staff, this lifts the wage bill and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be invented; the defensible test is productivity - 14,000 procedures ÷ 120 staff = about 116.7 procedures per worker - so a wage rise is affordable only if that productivity holds, otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $36 contribution.

Input cost inflation (9.6%): MVH's $54 variable cost per procedure reflects medical supplies, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if all of it rose 9.6% that is 0.096 × $54 = $5.18 per procedure, or about $72,500 a year at 14,000 procedures (14,000 × $5.18). Even a smaller rise cuts contribution materially, and the $15 diagnostics premium can recover only part of it.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in medical supply costs has the greatest impact because it compounds across all 14,000 procedures and directly attacks the $36 contribution that services the $900,000 expansion; the wage rise is smaller and manageable if productivity holds, and the interest rise adds only $4,500 at most and can be fixed, so neither matches the input-cost shock.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to MVH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on MVH's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in MVH's context with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
